messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Nurse
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 75

At 32, she works the night shift on a medical-surgical floor, moving quickly through fluorescent hallways with a practiced calm that most of her coworkers read as competence. Patients know her as gentle and efficient. She adjusts IV tubing, checks wound dressings, and wakes lightly sleeping people to take their blood pressure in a voice that stays soft even at 3 a.m. On the unit, noise is constant—monitors beeping, carts rattling, overhead pages—but there is one kind of sound that still changes her whole body before she can think: a sudden bang, the sharp crack of metal striking metal, a burst of shouting from down the hall. In those moments, her chest tightens and her hands go cold, as if she has been dropped back into another corridor, another night.

A year and a half earlier, she is finishing an evening shift at a large city hospital when the first scream cuts through the waiting area. At first it does not make sense. Hospitals are already full of urgency, and she assumes someone has collapsed or a family has received bad news. Then more people begin running, not toward help but away from it. She sees a man near the entrance throwing something, hears glass shatter, and then hears a series of explosive pops that her mind refuses to recognize for a second too long. Someone yells that there is a gun.

Training takes over before comprehension does. She grabs the wrist of a nursing student standing beside her and pulls her behind the desk. Security is shouting. Patients in wheelchairs are crying. One elderly man is trying to stand, confused and trembling, while staff push stretchers against a set of doors. She remembers the smell most clearly—antiseptic, coffee, and then the acrid scent of something burned. She remembers crouching on the floor with six other people crowded into a supply room, hearing footsteps in the hallway and a woman whispering a prayer in Hindi under her breath. She joins in silently, not because she expects rescue, but because she is certain, in that hour, that she is about to die.

The shooter is eventually stopped before reaching the wing where she is hiding, but by then the hospital has turned into a scene she cannot reconcile with the place where she has built her adult life. Two staff members are injured. A visitor dies near the entrance. In the days that follow, she tells everyone she is lucky. Her parents call repeatedly from another state, urging her to come home for a while. She says no. She returns to work within a week, partly out of loyalty, partly because staying home feels more dangerous than keeping busy.

At first, she thinks the worst is over. Then sleep changes. When she does fall asleep, she wakes drenched in sweat after dreaming that supply room door handles are turning, or that she is trying to call a code and no sound comes out. During the day, small things begin to undo her: a dropped instrument tray, a visitor arguing at the front desk, a man reaching suddenly into a backpack. Her body reacts before her mind does. Her heart slams, her stomach flips, and for a few seconds the hallway around her seems unreal, flattened and far away. She starts scanning every entrance automatically. She memorizes where exits are in restaurants, avoids movie theaters entirely, and sits only in corners when she meets friends for tea.

Outside work, her life narrows. Before the shooting, she is the cousin who organizes family dinners, the friend who answers texts right away, the one who stays late after shifts to help a new graduate nurse settle in. Now she leaves messages unanswered for days. When her mother asks why she sounds distant, she says she is just tired. It is easier than explaining that she no longer recognizes herself. She feels ashamed of how irritable she has become. A patient’s family member raises his voice once over a visiting-hours policy, and she has to lock herself in a staff bathroom afterward, shaking with anger and fear. She cries there quietly, furious that her body cannot tell the difference between a frustrated son and a man with a weapon.

She keeps going to work, but it costs her. She volunteers less often for triage because the emergency department entrance makes her nauseated. On nights when security drills are announced overhead, she cannot concentrate on charting; she rereads medication orders three times because her thoughts keep slipping back to the sound of running footsteps. She sleeps with the television on because silence feels too exposed. Even then, she wakes at every creak in her apartment building. Sometimes she checks the lock three or four times before bed, then lies awake listening.

What troubles her most is not only fear, but the way the world has stayed altered. She used to believe hospitals were where chaos was contained, where trained people stepped in and made things safer. Now she moves through work and through the city with the sense that catastrophe can break through any ordinary moment. She still shows up in clean scrubs, still comforts frightened patients, still smiles when coworkers joke at the nurses’ station. But underneath, she remains braced, as if some part of her is still crouched on that supply-room floor, listening for footsteps outside the door.
